Gaza Board of Peace says it will hand keys to UN if Israel fails to honour commitments
A senior adviser to the Trump-appointed Gaza Peace Council has warned that the body could return responsibility for the enclave to the United Nations if Israel does not honour its commitments under the 20-point plan, Israeli outlet Ynet has reported.
Josh Gruenbaum, who was appointed to the council by Trump and previously worked in the White House, told Ynet: “We have been extremely patient and have given Israel its space. But it is frustrating that now with the elections behind us — even if they haven’t resulted in a clear coalition — that Israel is failing to move forward on the commitments Netanyahu made to President Trump.”
“If this political leadership says it no longer wants to honour what they committed to, just let us know,” Gruenbaum said “And we will throw the keys back to the UN.”
Ynet said it had seen a presentation prepared by council members, who visited Israel last week. Its final slide, titled “Other alternatives to Gaza”, reportedly lists several scenarios if the plan is abandoned.
These include a future US administration and Congress ordering a different reconstruction plan, the UN Security Council taking over “perhaps through UNRWA”, the Palestinian Authority and Hamas.
The last scenario, according to the slide, is that Israel becomes fully responsible for the administrative and humanitarian costs of Gaza’s population.
Another slide reportedly says Hamas formally accepted the plan in July, pledging to give up its weapons and transfer governmental powers to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body meant to run the territory.
“We are at a standstill due to political elements within the Netanyahu government who have prevented us from progressing and from testing whether Hamas will keep its word,” Gruenbaum said, according to Ynet.
Gruenbaum also criticises Israel for failing to allow sufficient aid into Gaza before winter

Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says
Calls on the Israeli authorities to protect Palestinian olive farmers and ensure they can reach their groves safely have not been acted upon, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said, citing the Humanitarian Country Team.
Instead, in the first nine months of 2026, Israeli authorities uprooted or otherwise damaged more than 10,000 Palestinian-owned trees and saplings across the West Bank, mostly olives, the statement adds.
The Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which brings together UN bodies and humanitarian NGOs, said more than 400 Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest since September have resulted in casualties or damage to property, including to more than 4,000 trees and saplings.
The number of attacks this year exceeds that recorded in any previous olive harvest season. This year’s harvesting window is closing, the team said, but there is still some time to act.
"Humanitarian NGOs and UN agencies urge the Israeli authorities in the strongest possible terms: end all attacks on Palestinians and their livelihoods, as required by international law. Ensure farmers have free, safe, sufficient and reliable access to their land. The team added that perpetrators must be stopped and held to account," the statement read.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said six attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in the past week, while shipping traffic remained about 65 percent below pre-war levels.
In its weekly report published on Friday, UKMTO said four of the six incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and two in the Arabian Gulf.
The UKMTO recorded 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits during the seven days to November 18, including US-facilitated movements. The combined figure was down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound the previous week.
Around half of Strait of Hormuz transits involved energy carriers. Most vessels broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route, although UKMTO noted an increase in traffic along the southern route.
No attacks were recorded in the past week in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandab, with the last confirmed attack recorded on August 24. However, vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb remain about 22 percent below levels existing before 22 July when Houthis announced a blockade.

Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February had been the president’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States”.
After the midterm elections, Vance blamed the war for the Republicans’ historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict.
His statement, posted on social media, was widely seen as a break with Trump as the vice president weighs a 2028 White House bid.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”
Trump said on Friday that he was not unhappy with Vance’s conclusion but that it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgement that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.
“People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion,” Trump said. “But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they’re crazy.”
Vice President JD Vance on Iran: "The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsored terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands potentially, of innocent people. The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the President of the United States."

Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
Iran still has hope that diplomacy can end its war with the United States, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, adding that the two sides are still exchanging messages through mediators.
“We are seeking an agreement with the US that would ensure there is no further war afterwards,” Araghchi told an Iranian newspaper.
He said Tehran saw no need to change the intermediaries in the talks.
Before going any further, Iran wants guarantees that Washington is serious about negotiating, he said, and it has discussed the form and nature of possible confidence-building measures with the mediators.
Iran’s first demand is for US President Donald Trump to state explicitly that he wants an agreement, Araghchi said.
He added that it was not surprising for Trump to take a new position every day, or even to reverse what he had said the day before.
One of Iran’s red lines is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country, Araghchi stated, though he believed a fair solution could be reached.
He also said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US met Iran’s seven conditions.
His comments came hours after Trump reiterated that the US had "total control" over the strait.
Iran’s official position on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons remains the same, and its nuclear doctrine has not changed, Araghchi added.

If US President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business.
The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through Iran first.
“The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye.
Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. The first-ever US-Russia-China summit produced a thin declaration, and no carve-up of the world. But the format itself - three powers, one table, no Europeans - might matter more than anything they signed.
In February 1945, US President Franklin Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta to settle the shape of the postwar world.
Eight decades later, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen for the first trilateral meeting ever held among the leaders of the US, China and Russia.
The comparison was irresistible. Yet after roughly 90 minutes of talks, what emerged was far more modest: a four-point joint “Declaration toward Peace”. The statement’s text suggests that what was supposed to be a historic event was mostly just a photo op.
This brings to mind another photograph, one that adorned the front page of The New York Times a quarter of a century ago, during a United Nations summit in New York in September 2000 that was meant to mark the beginning of a new era focused on “Millennium Development Goals”.
Instead of picturing the General Assembly Hall, the newspaper used an image of the leaders of the UN Security Council’s five permanent members around a table outside the summit - conveying to readers exactly who was really running the show.

Climate justice campaigners have hit out at the draft outcome of the global climate talks, describing it as the “worst” in the conference’s history.
The draft agreement, which outlines the key commitments of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, was stripped of all references to a phase-out of fossil fuels, but backed “accelerating carbon capture, utilisation and storage”, which civil society actors have derided as a “false solution” to climate breakdown.
“It's much weaker language across all fronts, and overall, when we look at it, it’s aggressive, it is backtracking, and it's not going to help developing countries," Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told Middle East Eye.
"Rather, it is going to help the private sector, fossil fuel industry, and that is not what we came here for,” Singh said.
The “cover decision” is an overarching text which summarises the different negotiation outcomes, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement.
An initial draft which appeared on Monday was heavily edited, with many of the main commitments, including a transition away from fossil fuels and a $120bn target for finance to help developing countries adapt to the climate crisis, stripped out.
Crucially, the latest text substitutes a commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” for a pledge to “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience”.
The new draft also centres controversial carbon capture technologies, pledging to increase them 20- to 40-fold by 2035.

A year after the so-called ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, Palestinian and Israeli cinemas have been scrambling to capture a volatile reality shaped by questions more complex than those that emerged in the immediate aftermath of 7 October.
Maintaining one’s dignity while surviving a sadistically dehumanising campaign targeting civilians was the central preoccupation of the handful of films about Gaza released between 2024 and early 2026.
The 2026 autumn season, however, offers a different set of inquiries: the deeply asymmetrical power dynamics between the Israeli aggressor and the Palestinians; the viability of what has now become the wistful dream of a two-state solution; the lingering ache for a lost, irretrievable homeland; and the newly exposed, unflattering realities of Gaza’s informal economy.
As the colossal success of NAZA has made evident, Gaza will continue to dominate cinema's narrative on Palestine for the foreseeable future.
Yet, as this fall's crop of films suggests, new dimensions will gradually come into focus as Palestinian filmmakers continue to grapple with uncertain terrain post-7 October.

The US-Israeli war on Iran has “crushed” confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable waterway for the export of energy, Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), has warned.
“I don’t see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in February 2026,” Birol wrote for The Economist magazine in an essay published on Wednesday.
“Shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been blocked once, with a hugely disruptive effect on oil and gas markets. It can happen again. Confidence in the Strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed,” he added.
Birol said that the world "can conceivably manage without the strait," but it would be "difficult".
In its World Energy Outlook report published on Thursday, the IEA said developing alternative pipelines around the waterway would require around $40bn. This would add around $2 to the cost of a barrel of oil exported from the Middle East. An additional $200bn would need to be spent on alternative sources of energy outside the Middle East.
The IEA said that in the case of oil alone, new pipeline projects are under construction or consideration in the Middle East that could pump around seven million barrels per day of oil, allowing producers to reach international markets without going through the strait.

The election results were a decisive rebuke of the Trump administration's domestic and foreign policy, as Vice President JD Vance himself acknowledged the very next day.
Trump has previously just ignored the two successful resolutions stipulating that only Congress has the authority to declare - and thereby fund - the US at war.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague are scheduled to deliver a judgment on Thursday in a case brought by The Gambia accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority.
If the court rules in Gambia's favour, it will be the first time the United Nations' top court has held a state fully responsible for committing genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
It will be also be the first judgment in a case with large-scale intervention by third states.
On 11 November 2019, the Gambia filed its case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
It was the first time a state not directly affected had brought a genocide case before the court.
Eleven states have intervened, filing submissions on how the Genocide Convention should be interpreted, but mainly in support of the Gambia's case rather than as parties. The states, also present at the court on Thursday, are: Belgium, Canada, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, the Republic of Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom.
The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal.
Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.
Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

The New York Times (NYT) is facing widespread criticism over its report claiming that some of Iran's water infrastructure may have been built to support its missile programme, with critics accusing the newspaper of promoting war propaganda and providing a justification for attacks on Iranian civilian infrastructure.
Published on Monday with the headline "War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason", the article examines the geographical overlap between dam and water infrastructure projects and sites recently struck during the US-Israeli war on Iran. It suggests that some of these projects may have been designed, at least in part, to support military facilities.
One of the two journalists who wrote the piece, Sanam Mahoozi, shared the article on X, writing: “Why has Iran kept building dams amid a severe water crisis? @ErikaSolomon and I examined a striking overlap between water projects and military sites. Could some have served a dual purpose? No conclusive evidence, but questions worth exploring.”
The Iranian Water Diplomacy Association noted on Tuesday "with serious concern" the discrepancies in the report, including the fact that geographical proximity between struck sites and water infrastructure sites does not establish military use.
The report refers to 533 identified dams, but without any statistical analysis, it "has no evidentiary value", the association said. "Historical chronology also does not fit the hypothesis."
"Presenting water infrastructure as military, without credible evidence, blurs the line between civilian objects and military targets in public opinion and normalizes a threat-based view of facilities on which millions depend," the association said in its statement published online.

US judge rules in favour of foreign students and journalists after Trump limits visas
A US federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's attempt to limit visas for international students and members of the foreign press after university and media unions filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in August.
Massachusetts District Judge Dennis Saylor said on Monday that the government has been unable to prove there has been widespread visa fraud or national security concerns with this particular visa programme.
DHS's move to impose restrictions "is arbitrary and capricious", Saylor said in his decision.
"The Final Rule, entitled Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media... is hereby VACATED," he wrote.
Saylor added that DHS is "seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity - providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States - that Congress sought to permit and encourage".
The ruling preserves the "duration of status" or "D/S" stamp that international students receive on their visas and, by extension, on the visas foreign journalists receive as well.
It means they are legally permitted to stay in the country as long as they remain in the status they obtained, either as active students or working journalists, whether it's mere months or several years.

Tim Hortons app sending user data to Israeli cybertech company, advocacy group confirms
The Tim Hortons app has been sharing sensitive user data with Forter, an Israeli cybertech company founded by alumni of the Israeli military's infamous intelligence Unit 8200, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) has confirmed.
An investigation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) published last week found that the coffee chain app sends data to third-party companies overseas as soon as the app is launched.
Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science at the University of Calgary who scanned the app's network traffic with his team, said the third party built into the app receives enough information to create a digital fingerprint of each device that can be identified later.
Some of the data includes the device's name and unique identifier, details of the device's camera and sensors, and the names of Wi-Fi routers nearby, which can be used to determine the user's location.
"This was beyond the pale," Reardon told the CBC.
Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst, told the CBC that the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service, but the amount of data collected "seems quite excessive" for simply purchasing a cup of coffee.
In its published investigation, CBC did not identify the third party or its location, saying that "accountability rests with the app developer".
